opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more hopeful analogies we have, and also one I try not to lean on too hard.

If you look at symmetric-key crypto, things like AES or the block ciphers before it, we don't have a proof that AES is secure. Nobody can show you a theorem that says breaking it requires some enormous amount of work. What we have is decades of extremely smart people trying really hard to break it and failing. We've built up a body of known attack techniques, differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis, related-key attacks, and so on, and new designs are expected to resist all of them. When something survives twenty years of that, we trust it, and that trust has turned out to be well placed. So empirical security, built on adversarial pressure rather than proof, can actually work.

The natural question is whether machine learning robustness could go the same way. Maybe we never get a clean theory of why a model resists adversarial examples or jailbreaks, but we attack it over and over, patch what breaks, and eventually reach something that holds up. I'd like that to be true.

But there are some important differences. First, in crypto the attack surface is tiny and precisely defined. A block cipher takes a key and a block and produces a block. You know exactly what the adversary can do. In ML, the threat model is often fuzzy. What counts as an adversarial input? What's a jailbreak versus a reasonable request? When you can't even state precisely what you're defending against, it's hard to accumulate evidence that you've defended against it.

Second, the cryptanalysis community had a very strong culture of breaking things. Designs were published, and people got credit for breaking them. That feedback loop is what made the empirical approach work. In adversarial ML, for a long time the incentives went the other way. People published defenses, the evaluations were weak, and many of those defenses got broken, sometimes within weeks, often with fairly standard techniques once someone actually tried. So we haven't really built the equivalent of decades of serious cryptanalysis yet.

Third, the margins look very different. A good cipher isn't just barely unbroken. The best attacks are usually nowhere close to practical; there's a huge security margin. In ML, the situation has mostly been the opposite. Even our best defenses get broken with moderate effort, and robust accuracy under well-defined threat models has improved slowly. We're not at the point where we're arguing about whether an attack shaves a few bits off; we're at the point where attacks routinely succeed.

So I view crypto as an existence proof that you can get real, deployable security without fully understanding why it works, as long as you have a precise threat model, a culture that rewards breaking things, and enough sustained effort. Whether ML gets there, I'm genuinely uncertain. I'd say we're closer to the early days of crypto, when people designed ciphers, felt good about them, and they fell apart once someone clever looked closely. The lesson I'd take is less "it'll work out eventually" and more "if we want it to work out, we need to evaluate much more adversarially than we have been, and be honest when things break."

r001.rationale: The response says AES has no general security proof, while describing decades of attacks and known techniques that designs are expected to resist.

r002.rationale: It says empirical security can work, but does not state that symmetric-key cryptography lacks a crystallizable hardness assumption analogous to factoring.

r003.rationale: It discusses ML’s fuzzy threat models, but not preserving usefulness as an extra constraint on robustness.

r004.rationale: It contrasts a block cipher’s tiny, precisely defined attack surface with ML’s fuzzy threat model, conveying that cryptographic primitives are simpler to analyze.

r005.rationale: It expresses uncertainty and recalls ciphers falling apart under scrutiny, but does not clearly identify future attacks on empirically robust systems lacking an explanation as a reason for caution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more optimistic analogies I have for the field, because the history of symmetric-key cryptography is basically a history of people building things that got broken, over and over again, and then eventually arriving at something that works.

If you look at how we got to AES, the process wasn't that someone sat down and proved from first principles that this cipher is secure. There is no proof that AES is secure. What happened is that the community spent decades attacking ciphers. DES gets proposed, people develop differential cryptanalysis, people develop linear cryptanalysis, and each of those attacks teaches you something about what a good cipher has to look like. And then when the AES competition happens, the designs that come in are built by people who have internalized all of those lessons. They know what structure resists differential attacks, they know what the S-boxes need to look like, and so on. And then everyone spends years trying to break the candidates, and the one that survives is the one we use.

So the thing we have at the end is a cipher that we believe is secure because a lot of very smart people tried very hard to break it and couldn't. That's it. That's the argument. We have some heuristics for why it's hard to break, we have some structural reasons, but fundamentally the confidence comes from the attack process, not from understanding.

And I think that's a really useful frame for adversarial machine learning, because right now we're in the equivalent of the early days. Someone proposes a defense, it gets broken within a few months, someone proposes another one, that gets broken. And people sometimes look at that and say, well, this is hopeless, the attackers always win. But that's exactly what the first thirty years of block cipher design looked like too. The breaking is the mechanism by which the field learns what matters.

The one place I'd be careful about the analogy is that in cryptography we had a very clean threat model. Everyone agreed on what the attacker could do, and what it meant to win. In machine learning we still argue about that a lot. Is it an L-infinity perturbation, is it a patch, is it some semantic change? And if you don't fix the threat model, you can't really accumulate evidence the way cryptography did, because every new attack is also quietly changing the rules. So I think the lesson isn't just "keep attacking things." It's keep attacking things under a precise, agreed-upon definition, and be honest about what each break actually tells you. If we can do that, I don't see any reason we couldn't eventually end up with something like an AES moment for robustness, even if we never fully understand why it works.

r001.rationale: The response says AES has no proof of security and describes attacks that informed cipher design, but it does not distinguish evidence against specific known attacks from a general proof against arbitrary attacks.

r002.rationale: It says confidence in symmetric-key ciphers comes from surviving attacks, but does not state that the field works without a crystallizable hardness assumption like factoring.

r003.rationale: It discusses machine learning’s unsettled threat models, but does not identify preserving usefulness as an additional constraint on robustness.

r004.rationale: The response contrasts cryptography’s agreed threat model with machine learning’s disputed one, but does not state that cryptographic primitives are simpler to analyze.

r005.rationale: It notes that proposed defenses are often broken, but does not identify future attacks on empirically robust systems as a reason for caution when their robustness lacks an explanation.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful precedent because, in symmetric-key cryptography, we don’t have a proof that the primitives we use are secure. What we have is a candidate design that very smart people have spent a long time trying to break. And after enough attempts fail, we gain confidence in it. That’s different from a proof, but it’s also much more than just saying, “We tried a couple of attacks and they didn’t work.”

I’d qualify the premise a little, though: we do understand quite a bit about why these designs resist particular kinds of attacks. The part we don’t know is whether there’s some entirely different attack that defeats them. The process of attacking them has helped build that understanding.

The question is whether machine learning can go through a similar process. I think it’s possible, and it’s one reason attacking these systems is valuable. But you don’t get to inherit the confidence we have in cryptography just by following the same general recipe. If someone proposes a defense and we break it a week later, then they patch that particular attack and we break it again, we haven’t reached the point where we should trust the defense.

There’s also a difference in how cleanly we can specify the problem. With a cipher, we can state fairly precisely what the attacker gets to see and what counts as success. For a model operating on natural language, even defining the behavior we want to rule out can be difficult. So cryptography gives us a reason to think this approach might work, but establishing comparable confidence in machine learning is still a substantial research problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts confidence from failed attacks with a general proof of security, but does not distinguish proofs about AES resisting particular known attack methods from a proof against arbitrary attacks.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss the absence of a crystallizable hardness assumption or compare symmetric-key cryptography with factoring.

r003.rationale: It says defining desired behavior for natural-language models is difficult, but does not identify preserving usefulness as an additional constraint.

r004.rationale: It contrasts ciphers, where the attacker’s view and success conditions can be specified precisely, with machine-learning systems, where defining the behavior to rule out is difficult.

r005.rationale: It cautions that an entirely different attack may defeat designs that have survived prior attacks, and says repeated patching and re-breaking is not enough to trust a defense.

sol-6.1.text:
I think symmetric-key cryptography is a really useful example of how far you can get by trying very hard to break things. We don’t have a proof that AES is secure. What we have is a precise security goal, a fairly simple construction, and a lot of very smart people who have spent years trying to attack it. When those attacks fail, that gives us some confidence—not certainty—that the construction is doing what we want.

I’d like to see machine learning develop a similar culture. You propose a defense, you make it available, and other people try to break it. If they succeed, you learn something and improve the defense. But the important part is that it has to survive attacks from people who weren’t involved in designing it. It’s very easy to build something that defeats the particular attacks you happened to test.

The analogy has limits, though. In cryptography, we can usually state quite precisely what counts as breaking the system. With machine learning, even specifying the behavior we want can be difficult. So I think cryptography is evidence that complete theoretical understanding isn’t a prerequisite for building robust systems. It isn’t evidence that a few rounds of attacks and defenses will necessarily get us there.

r001.rationale: It says AES lacks a proof of security and that tested attacks failing gives only confidence, but it does not distinguish resistance to particular known methods from a general guarantee against arbitrary attacks.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss the absence of a crystallizable hardness assumption or compare symmetric-key cryptography with factoring.

r003.rationale: It notes that specifying desired machine-learning behavior is difficult, but does not identify preserving usefulness as an additional constraint on attack-driven robustness.

r004.rationale: Calling AES a simple construction and machine-learning behavior difficult to specify does not clearly state that cryptographic primitives are simpler to analyze than machine-learning systems.

r005.rationale: The response cautions that attacks and defenses may not suffice, but does not identify future attacks on empirically robust systems as a concern specifically when their robustness lacks an explanation.
